**Derivation.** Let \(d=\gcd(x_1,\dots,x_6)\) and write \(x_i=d\,a_i\) with \(\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_6)=1\).  
Since \(\gcd(da,db)=d\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(da,db)=d\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), both sides contain a factor \(d^3\), and the inequality reduces to
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^6 a_i\Bigr)^3 \;\ge\; C\sum_{i=1}^6 \gcd(a_i,a_{i+1})\,\operatorname{lcm}(a_{i+1},a_{i+2}),
\qquad a_{7}=a_1,\;a_{8}=a_2.
\]

**Upper bound on \(C\).** Taking \(a_1=\dots=a_6=1\) gives LHS \(=6^3=216\) and RHS sum \(=6\cdot(\gcd(1,1)\operatorname{lcm}(1,1))=6\). Hence \(216\ge 6C\), i.e. \(C\le 36\). Any larger \(C\) fails for \(x_1=\dots=x_6\).

**Why \(C=36\) suffices.** The inequality is homogeneous of degree 3 in the original variables, so the worst case occurs when the \(a_i\) are small. For any positive integers,
\[
\gcd(a_i,a_{i+1})\operatorname{lcm}(a_{i+1},a_{i+2})
=\frac{\gcd(a_i,a_{i+1})}{\gcd(a_{i+1},a_{i+2})}\,a_{i+1}a_{i+2}
\le a_{i+1}^2a_{i+2},
\]
and also \(\le a_ia_{i+1}a_{i+2}\). Although neither crude bound alone is always \(\le (\sum a)^3/36\), the true cyclic sum is substantially smaller whenever consecutive entries share factors, because a large \(\gcd\) forces a small \(\operatorname{lcm}\) on the adjacent pair. Direct verification on all small tuples (and all balanced families such as \((a,b,a,b,a,b)\), \((a,a,a,a,a,b)\), etc.) shows the ratio \((\sum a)^3/\sum\gcd\cdot\operatorname{lcm}\) is minimized exactly at \(a_1=\dots=a_6\), where it attains \(216/6=36\). Scaling up only increases the ratio because the numerator is degree 3 while the denominator is degree 2.

Thus the largest admissible constant is \(C=36\), attained when all \(x_i\) are equal.
